name: Psyllium husk
summary: Gel-forming soluble fibre from Plantago seed husks; well studied for constipation and cholesterol, with only minor weight-loss effects reported.
lead: Psyllium, also called ispaghula or isabgol, is obtained from seeds of Plantago species, chiefly Plantago ovata. The seed coat is milled into a white husk that absorbs water to form a gel; the gel-forming polysaccharide has been characterised chemically.  India produces most of the world supply.

name: Apple cider vinegar
summary: Fermented apple juice drunk diluted for fat loss and clear skin; trials are small and major references describe no good evidence for weight loss.
lead: Apple cider vinegar (ACV) is a vinegar made from apple juice by two-step fermentation: yeast convert sugars to alcohol, then acetic acid bacteria convert the alcohol to acetic acid. The finished product is roughly 94 percent water and 5 percent acetic acid with almost no fat, protein or micronutrients. Unfiltered versions contain a cloudy cellulose-and-bacteria sediment called the mother.
claims: Drinking ACV burns fat and sculpts the body
ACV toner clears acne and balances skin pH
ACV rinses improve hair and remove dandruff
Gut health via fermented foods like ACV is a root driver of looks

name: Green coffee bean extract
summary: Unroasted-coffee chlorogenic acid pill sold for fat loss; the best-known supporting study was retracted and the FTC acted against marketers.
lead: Green coffee bean extract (GCE) is a concentrate of unroasted coffee beans, standardised in supplements to chlorogenic acid, a polyphenol that is largely lost in roasting.  It has been sold as a weight-loss supplement and studied for blood pressure and metabolic markers.

name: Chromium picolinate
summary: Chromium supplement sold to curb cravings and cut fat; reviews report no reliable evidence of weight or muscle effects.
lead: Chromium(III) picolinate is a pink-red coordination compound of trivalent chromium and picolinic acid, sold as a dietary supplement and marketed in the United States to athletes for muscle development and for weight loss.

name: Detox / slimming teas
summary: Herbal teas, often senna-based, sold to cleanse or slim; the weight change is typically fluid, and a 2015 review found no compelling evidence for detox claims.
lead: Detox or slimming teas are herbal beverages sold to cleanse the body of toxins or aid weight loss; many contain senna, an anthraquinone plant laxative.

name: Laxatives for weight loss
summary: Using laxatives to drop scale weight; reviews say the loss is mostly water, and use is linked to later eating disorders and electrolyte harms.
lead: Laxative use for weight control means taking laxatives not to treat constipation but to reduce body weight.  It is classified in clinical literature as a purging behaviour associated with eating disorders.

name: Compounded semaglutide / microdosing GLP-1
summary: Pharmacy-made or gray-market semaglutide, often used at below-label amounts; the fat-loss drug is proven at approved doses, the microdosing version is not.
lead: Compounded semaglutide is semaglutide, the active ingredient in the approved drugs Ozempic, Wegovy and Rybelsus, that a compounding pharmacy has prepared as a custom product rather than the manufacturer's branded pen or tablet. "Microdosing" GLP-1 refers to an informal practice in which people use amounts smaller than the doses on the approved label, often drawn from multi-dose vials, with the stated aims of reducing appetite and body fat with fewer side effects or lower cost.
claims: Taking less than the labeled dose gives most of the appetite benefit with fewer side effects.
Compounded semaglutide is equivalent to the branded drug.
Combining GLP-1 use with extended fasting speeds fat loss.

name: Calorie deficit / calorie counting
summary: Eating below maintenance and logging it: the standard way to lose fat, with limited evidence specific to facial appearance.
lead: A calorie deficit means eating less energy than the body uses, and calorie counting is the practice of tracking food intake, usually with an app or scale, to maintain that gap. In looksmaxxing communities it is the baseline method for losing body fat to reveal facial and body definition, often called "cutting."
claims: A modest deficit loses fat while keeping muscle and hair, whereas extreme deficits harm both.

name: High-protein diet
summary: Protein-forward eating for muscle retention and fullness; supported for those goals, untested for hair or skin claims.
lead: A high-protein diet emphasizes protein-rich foods such as meat, fish, eggs, dairy and legumes. Definitions vary: Wikipedia describes it as drawing 40 percent or more of daily calories from protein, while other sources use thresholds above the US recommended dietary allowance of 0.8 grams per kilogram of body weight per day, or around 1.2 to 2.0 g/kg for active people.
claims: Very high protein intake improves hair, skin, collagen and other tissues beyond muscle.

name: OMAD (one meal a day)
summary: All daily food in one sitting: an intermittent-fasting variant with no OMAD-specific trials behind it.
lead: OMAD stands for "one meal a day", an eating pattern in which all daily food is consumed in a single sitting, usually within a one- to two-hour window. Wikipedia classifies it as a subtype of time-restricted eating within intermittent fasting.
claims: OMAD makes dieting easier because hunger is manageable and meals are larger.
OMAD at moderate calories does not cause hair loss, but extreme deficits do.

name: Extended water fasting
summary: Multi-day water-only fasts for fast scale loss; much early loss is lean tissue and refeeding carries documented risks.
lead: Extended or prolonged water fasting means consuming no food, only water, for more than 24 hours, typically five to twenty days in the literature. In looksmaxxing forums it is discussed for rapid fat loss before a cut or lean bulk, and for 2 to 7 day attempts.
claims: A multi-day water fast removes fat faster than a calorie deficit.

name: 5:2 diet / alternate-day fasting
summary: Two very low-calorie days a week, or every other day: weight loss comparable in scope to ordinary dieting, with limited evidence it does better.
lead: The 5:2 diet and alternate-day fasting are two forms of intermittent energy restriction. The 5:2 pattern has two non-consecutive days of roughly 500 to 600 calories and normal eating on the other five; alternate-day fasting alternates a very low-calorie day (under about 25 percent of usual needs) with a normal "feast" day, and a modified version allows up to 25 percent of calories on fast days.

name: Keto diet
summary: A very low-carb, high-fat diet used for fat loss; trials show short-term loss but little edge over other diets once calories are matched.
lead: The ketogenic (keto) diet is a very low-carbohydrate, high-fat, adequate-protein eating pattern that shifts the body toward burning fat and producing ketone bodies. It originated as a medical therapy for drug-resistant epilepsy, mainly in children, and has since become a mainstream weight-loss diet.
claims: Keto is the fastest way to lose fat and look leaner.
Keto harms the kidneys.
A high-fat keto diet raises cholesterol and does not raise testosterone.

name: Lion diet
summary: Beef, salt and water only: a carnivore-diet variant with no trials behind it and dietitian warnings about nutrient gaps.
lead: The lion diet is a restrictive elimination diet consisting only of ruminant meat (typically beef), salt and water. It is described as a stricter form of the carnivore diet, which allows animal products such as meat, dairy and eggs.

name: Carb cycling / refeeds
summary: Alternating high- and low-carb days to lean out; direct evidence is thin and fat loss tracks total calories.
lead: Carb cycling alternates higher-carbohydrate and lower-carbohydrate days, often around training, with higher-carbohydrate days sometimes called refeeds. Protein is usually kept roughly constant while fat is adjusted in the opposite direction to carbohydrate.

name: Volume eating
summary: Filling meals with low-calorie-density foods to stay full on fewer calories; plausible for dieting but unstudied as a looksmaxxing method.
lead: Volume eating is the practice of building meals around low-energy-density foods, such as vegetables and fruit, that supply a lot of food by weight or volume for relatively few calories, with the aim of feeling full while cutting calorie intake.

name: Avoiding ultra-processed foods
summary: A whole-food approach built on the NOVA scheme; linked to health outcomes in observational studies but no appearance trials.
lead: Avoiding ultra-processed foods (UPFs) is a whole-food dietary approach, sometimes used by people trying to lose fat, based on the NOVA food classification, in which UPFs are industrially manufactured products made from many ingredients, often including additives and ingredients rarely used in home cooking.

name: Cotton ball diet
summary: Swallowing cotton balls to feel full; condemned by health experts for blockage risk.
lead: The cotton ball diet is a fad diet in which people swallow cotton balls, sometimes dipped in juice or smoothies, to feel full without eating food.

name: Master Cleanse / juice cleanse
summary: Lemon-syrup or juice-only fasts used for quick de-bloating; medical sources report no evidence for detox claims and temporary weight loss.
lead: The Master Cleanse, also called the lemonade diet, is a modified juice fast in which followers consume no solid food and instead drink a mixture of lemon juice, maple syrup and cayenne pepper in water, along with tea and a daily salt-water drink. It was marketed by Stanley Burroughs from the 1940s and revived by his 1976 book The Master Cleanser. Juice cleanses more broadly restrict a person to fruit and vegetable juices for a period of usually one to seven days.
claims: A cleanse removes toxins and resets the body.
A cleanse produces fast weight loss and a leaner look.
Cleanses are harmless short-term.

name: Dehydration cuts / water cutting
summary: Sweating and fluid manipulation to look drier; borrowed from combat sports, where extreme cuts have contributed to deaths.
lead: Water cutting, or dehydration cutting, is the practice of losing body water over hours or days, typically by water manipulation, sweating, sweat suits or saunas, to weigh less or look leaner. It originates in weight-class sports such as combat sports and rowing, where athletes cut rapidly to make a weight limit. In looksmaxxing and physique communities the same idea is applied to look more defined for photos or events.
claims: Dropping water makes you look more shredded for a day.
Water cuts are safe if done briefly.

name: Zone 2 cardio
summary: Easy, steady cardio at conversational pace; popular, but little zone-specific research for appearance goals.
lead: Zone 2 cardio refers to low-to-moderate intensity steady aerobic exercise, in popular heart-rate-zone schemes the second zone, often described as a pace at which conversation remains possible. It has become popular in fitness and longevity communities and is discussed in looksmaxxing circles as a low-stress way to burn fat.

name: HIIT
summary: Short all-out interval workouts; well supported for fitness, with modest fat-loss effects similar to steady cardio.
lead: High-intensity interval training (HIIT) alternates short, near-maximal bursts of exercise with brief recovery periods, usually in sessions under 30 minutes. A related form, sprint interval training, uses all-out efforts. It is promoted in fitness and looksmaxxing circles as a time-efficient way to lose fat and improve conditioning.
claims: HIIT burns fat faster than steady cardio.
A few minutes is enough to improve fitness.

name: 10k steps / NEAT
summary: Raising daily steps and everyday movement; benefits are well supported for health, with fat-loss effects varying by person.
lead: The 10,000-steps-a-day target and non-exercise activity thermogenesis (NEAT) both concern raising everyday movement rather than formal exercise. NEAT is the energy used for activities outside structured exercise, such as standing, walking, chores and fidgeting. Looksmaxxing communities discuss raising daily steps as a way to support fat loss.
claims: 10,000 steps a day is the necessary target.
Raising NEAT meaningfully helps fat loss.

name: 12-3-30 incline walking
summary: Viral 12% incline, 3 mph, 30 minute treadmill walk; only one small exploratory study exists.
lead: The 12-3-30 workout is a treadmill routine named for its settings: a 12 percent incline, a speed of 3 miles per hour and 30 minutes of walking. It spread through social media and is discussed in looksmaxxing and fitness circles as a low-impact fat-loss routine.
claims: 12-3-30 is an effective fat-loss routine.

name: Rucking
summary: Walking with a loaded backpack; popular as low-impact cardio, with no appearance-specific trials behind it.
lead: Rucking is the practice of walking or hiking while carrying a weighted backpack (a rucksack) as a form of exercise. The term comes from military usage, where a "ruck march" or loaded march is a fast march over distance carrying kit; the civilian fitness version has been promoted as a low-impact way to raise the effort of walking.
claims: Rucking burns far more calories than walking and nearly as many as jogging.
Rucking improves bone density and muscular endurance.
Loaded marching carries injury risk when load or distance is increased quickly.

name: Fasted cardio
summary: Morning cardio before eating, a bodybuilding cutting habit with little direct research in the sources reviewed.
lead: Fasted cardio is aerobic exercise performed after an overnight fast, typically first thing in the morning before eating. It is a staple of bodybuilding-style cutting phases, where practitioners believe that exercising with low carbohydrate stores increases the share of energy drawn from body fat.

name: Sauna / sweat suits
summary: Sweating in heat-trapping gear or a sauna: it moves water weight temporarily and has little direct fat-loss research.
lead: Sauna suits are non-breathable garments, and saunas are heated rooms, used while exercising or resting to provoke heavy sweating. Practitioners use them for temporary weight loss and in some circles believe the sweating burns fat or flushes it out; the weight lost is mostly water, which returns with rehydration.

name: Spot reduction exercises
summary: Ab or face exercises meant to burn local fat; studies reported by reference works find fat loss is systemic.
lead: Spot reduction is the belief that exercising a particular body area, such as crunches for the abdomen or facial exercises for the cheeks, preferentially burns fat stored over that area. It is widely marketed in fitness media, and in looksmaxxing communities it appears as ab routines and face or jaw exercises aimed at a leaner look.
claims: Doing ab exercises burns belly fat.
Facial exercises slim the face or jaw.
Adding core work to cardio may speed trunk fat loss.

name: Bulk and cut / body recomposition
summary: Cycling calorie surplus and deficit phases to add muscle and then lean out; borrowed from bodybuilding, little direct trial evidence in the sources.
lead: Bulking and cutting is a cyclical approach to physique change: a bulk is a period of eating in a calorie surplus to gain muscle, and a cut is a period in a deficit to lose fat while keeping as much muscle as possible. Body recomposition is the alternative of trying to lose fat and gain muscle at the same time.
claims: Cycling bulks and cuts avoids getting too fat.
An appetite-suppressing weight-loss drug can be combined with bulking for recomposition.
A slow recomposition with calorie and protein planning can reduce body fat while keeping muscle.

name: Macro tracking apps
summary: Food-logging apps like MyFitnessPal for hitting calorie and protein targets; popular, with self-report accuracy limits.
lead: Macro tracking apps let users log food and drink against daily calorie and macronutrient (protein, carbohydrate, fat) targets. The best-known example is MyFitnessPal, which describes itself as an app and website for looking up the nutritional content of foods, logging intake against goals, building meal plans and tracking exercise.
